environment.cre_risk0_pct.plain: Out of every 100 residents of each municipio, how many have none of the Census Bureau's disaster risk factors.

environment.cre_risk0_pct.definition: Residents with none of the risk factors, in percent of the residents the estimates cover. The risk factors are the Census Bureau's ten risk factors that make it harder to withstand and recover from a disaster: household income below 130% of the poverty line, only one or no adults aged 18 to 64 in the household, more than 0.75 people per room, limited English or no one with a high-school diploma in the household, no one employed full-time year-round, a disability, no health insurance, age 65 or over, no vehicle and no broadband.
environment.cre_risk0_pct.method: environment_series.py reads each release's Puerto Rico municipio file and the island row of its tract file and publishes the three shares (PRED0_PE, PRED12_PE, PRED3_PE) with their margins of error (_PM, 90% confidence).
environment.cre_risk0_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 14.74% in 2019 and 18.09% in 2024 (± 0.55 points). Highest in 2024: Dorado 27.0%, Guaynabo 26.5%, Barceloneta 24.3%.
caveats: Modeled estimates with margins of error: read the margin before comparing two places.
The ten factors are the same in every release, but from 2023 the Census Bureau computes municipio margins a new way (smaller), so compare margins across 2022 and 2023 with care.

One factor is a household where no one speaks English very well (or no one has a high-school diploma), so in Puerto Rico it counts many Spanish-speaking households and raises the shares with risk factors.
environment.cre_risk0_pct.source_detail: Census Bureau Community Resilience Estimates for Puerto Rico, files CRE{yy}_PR_MUNICIPIO.csv and CRE{yy}_PR.csv, 2019 and 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024

cutoff.cut_bridge_pct.plain: The share of residents who would have no road to a hospital if every bridge in poor condition, or already closed, were closed.
cutoff.cut_bridge_pct.plain_es: La proporción de residentes que se quedarían sin carretera hasta un hospital si se cerraran todos los puentes en malas condiciones o ya cerrados.
cutoff.cut_bridge_pct.definition: The share of the area's residents (2020 Census) who would have no road to any hospital if every bridge the National Bridge Inventory rates in poor condition, or lists as closed, were closed. An estimate and a worst case: the 1% flood everywhere at once and every flooded stretch closed, where a real storm raises only some rivers for a few hours. Expressways and sound bridges stay open. Landslides and fallen trees are not in the model. Vieques and Culebra, with no road to a hospital at all, are left out.
cutoff.cut_bridge_pct.method: cutoff.py places a test point every 25 m along every road of the graph the map uses (roads.bin, from OpenStreetMap) and closes each stretch whose points fall in FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area, except motorways and trunk roads (raised expressways) and the span of each bridge the National Bridge Inventory rates good or fair. Bridges in poor condition, and those listed as closed, close the road under their point. Each 2020 Census block with residents is placed on its nearest road joined to the network within 2 km; it is cut off when no open road leads from it to a hospital (the hospitals and medical centers of OpenStreetMap in the observatory's place index). A block whose own stretch is closed is cut off too. A barrio's or municipio's figure is the share of its residents, Vieques and Culebra left out.
cutoff.cut_bridge_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 0.1% (4,478 residents). Highest: Yabucoa (4.2%), Maunabo (2.7%), Cabo Rojo (1.5%). 355 bridges are in poor condition or closed; 339 road stretches close. Most communities have another way around.
caveats: Poor condition is the National Bridge Inventory's rating of the deck, superstructure or substructure: it does not mean the bridge will fail.
A bridge's point is placed on the nearest road within 60 m; where a bridge crosses over another road, the wrong one may close.
Hospitals are those of OpenStreetMap named hospital or medical center; a community health center (CDT or 330 center) is not one.
cutoff.cut_bridge_pct.source_detail: Estimated by the observatory: the OpenStreetMap road graph (roads.bin) with the roads in FEMA's flood area or under bridges in poor condition closed, and each 2020 Census block tested for an open road to a hospital (cutoff.py)

drought.drought_area_pct.plain: How much of each municipio was in drought, on average over the weeks of the year.
drought.drought_area_pct.plain_es: Qué parte de cada municipio estuvo en sequía, en promedio durante las semanas del año.
drought.drought_area_pct.definition: The share of the municipio's area in drought (moderate, D1, or worse) on the US Drought Monitor, averaged over the weeks of the year. 100 means the whole municipio was in drought every week. The Drought Monitor is drawn each week by experts from rainfall, soil moisture, stream flow, reservoir levels and reports; it is a judgment, not a measurement, and its lines follow no municipio. 2026 holds the weeks published so far (up to the map of 2026-11-10).
drought.drought_area_pct.method: drought.py reads, for each municipio and for Puerto Rico, the share of the area in each drought class on every weekly US Drought Monitor map since 2000-01-04 (cumulative shares: D1 means moderate drought or worse). For each year it averages the D1 share over the weeks, and counts the weeks in which D1, or D2, covered at least half the area. A year has 52 or 53 maps; 2026 holds the weeks published so far (to 2026-11-10).
drought.drought_area_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 0.1% in 2025; 26.5% in 2026 so far. The worst whole year was 2015 (28.5%); highest that year: Caguas (67.1%), Gurabo (66.2%), Guayama (65.9%). Most years before 2014 had little or none.
caveats: The Drought Monitor is drawn each week by experts from rainfall, soil moisture, stream flow, reservoir levels and reports: a judgment, not a measurement. Its lines do not follow municipio borders.
2026 is not a whole year: it holds the weeks to 2026-11-10, and grows each Thursday when the new map is published.
Drought on the map is not the same as water rationing: rationing depends on the reservoirs and the pipes that serve each place (see the reservoir layer).
drought.drought_area_pct.source_detail: US Drought Monitor, weekly maps 2000-01-04 to 2026-11-10. Data courtesy of NDMC, via https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu

environment.quakes_m25.plain: How many earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or more struck in or just off each municipio, every year.
environment.quakes_m25.plain_es: Cuántos terremotos de magnitud 2.5 o más ocurrieron en o frente a cada municipio, cada año.
environment.quakes_m25.definition: Earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or more in USGS's catalog whose epicenter is in the municipio or, offshore, nearest to it and within 25 km of its coast.
environment.quakes_m25.method: environment_series.py asks ComCat for every earthquake of magnitude 2.5 or more in a box around Puerto Rico each year. An earthquake counts in the municipio whose boundary holds its epicenter; offshore, in the nearest municipio if it is within 25 km of that municipio's coast, else not at all. Each earthquake counts once, so the municipal values add up to Puerto Rico's.
environment.quakes_m25.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 153 in 2000, 6,297 in 2020 (the southwest sequence; strongest 6.4) and 522 in 2025.
caveats: A count of events, not of damage: most are felt little or not at all.
The catalog records more small earthquakes in later years as the seismic network grew.

fires.fire_n.plain: How many times a satellite saw a grass or brush fire burning in the area during the year.
fires.fire_n.plain_es: Cuántas veces un satélite vio un fuego de pastos o maleza ardiendo en el área durante el año.
fires.fire_n.definition: The number of VIIRS active fire detections on NOAA-20 in the area in the calendar year that FIRMS tags as presumed vegetation fires with nominal or high confidence.
fires.fire_n.method: fires.py downloads FIRMS's yearly country files for Puerto Rico for NOAA-20 (VIIRS 375 m, standard processing; 2019-2025) and keeps the detections FIRMS tags as presumed vegetation fires (type 0) with nominal or high confidence. landslide.ls_land_high_pct.plain: How much of the land is in the three most landslide-prone classes of the USGS map: the places where intense rain is most likely to set off a slide.

landslide.ls_land_high_pct.definition: The share of the land that the USGS map of susceptibility to landslides triggered by intense rainfall (Hughes and Schulz, 2020) puts in its High, Very High or Extremely High class: the most susceptible 30% of the main island. Over all the land of the area that the map classifies, in percent.
landslide.ls_land_high_pct.method: landslide.py reads the 7,294 PNG tiles of zoom 15 that cover the main island (4.8 m a pixel in Web Mercator, about 4.5 m on the ground), turns each pixel's color back into its class (gray Low, yellow Moderate, orange High, red Very High, blue-violet Extremely High; the build stops on any other color) and counts each pixel's ground area in the barrio whose outline holds its center (or the nearest within about 1 km, for the generalized coast). No raster library is used: the PNGs are decoded with zlib and numpy. Checks against the report, run at every build: the classes cover 40.0, 30.0, 20.0, 9.0 and 1.0% of the 8,739 km2 classified (the report: 40, 30, 20, 9 and 1% of 8,700 km2), and the 71,431 slope failures of Hurricane María fall 1.2, 10.2, 29.4, 44.4 and 14.7% in the five classes (the report's table 5: 1.2, 10.0, 29.4, 44.6 and 14.9%), so the tiles are the published map. A barrio's share is the area of the three classes over all its classified area; a municipio's and Puerto Rico's shares come from the areas of their barrios. The share of each of the five classes is a dataset of its own (landslide.ls_cls_low_pct to landslide.ls_cls_extremely_high_pct).
landslide.ls_land_high_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico (the main island): 30.0%, by the map's design. Highest: Maricao (79.8%), Jayuya (70.4%), Las Marías (69.5%). 4 municipios have less than 0.5%, and 55 barrios have none; 229 barrios have half or more of their land in these classes.
caveats: A relative ranking within Puerto Rico, not a probability: the classes are set by area (the most susceptible 30% of the island is High or above), so 'high' means high compared with the rest of the island.

The map shows where landslides may start during or soon after intense rainfall; it does not show where a slide travels downhill, and deep bedrock slides and earthquake-triggered ones are poorly represented. It is not a substitute for a site-specific slope-stability study.
Vieques, Culebra and Isla de Mona are not in the USGS model: no value. Puerto Rico's figure is the main island's.

landslide.ls_res_high.method: landslide.py reads the 7,294 PNG tiles of zoom 15 that cover the main island (4.8 m a pixel in Web Mercator, about 4.5 m on the ground), turns each pixel's color back into its class (gray Low, yellow Moderate, orange High, red Very High, blue-violet Extremely High; the build stops on any other color) and counts each pixel's ground area in the barrio whose outline holds its center (or the nearest within about 1 km, for the generalized coast). No raster library is used: the PNGs are decoded with zlib and numpy. Checks against the report, run at every build: the classes cover 40.0, 30.0, 20.0, 9.0 and 1.0% of the 8,739 km2 classified (the report: 40, 30, 20, 9 and 1% of 8,700 km2), and the 71,431 slope failures of Hurricane María fall 1.2, 10.2, 29.4, 44.4 and 14.7% in the five classes (the report's table 5: 1.2, 10.0, 29.4, 44.6 and 14.9%), so the tiles are the published map. Each 2020 census block with residents counts whole in the class of the pixel under its internal point (the point the Census Bureau guarantees lies inside the block), in the barrio whose outline holds the point; a municipio is the sum of its barrios. A block that a class edge crosses is counted on one side, so a barrio's figure is rough (the same rule as the exposure series). 1,080 residents live in blocks whose point falls on a pixel the map leaves unclassified (the coast) and count as not in these classes.
landslide.ls_res_high.how_to_read: Puerto Rico (the main island): about 375,779 residents in 2020. Most: Naranjito (17,078), Utuado (15,269), Mayagüez (13,959).
caveats: A relative ranking within Puerto Rico, not a probability: the classes are set by area (the most susceptible 30% of the island is High or above), so 'high' means high compared with the rest of the island.

The map shows where landslides may start during or soon after intense rainfall; it does not show where a slide travels downhill, and deep bedrock slides and earthquake-triggered ones are poorly represented. It is not a substitute for a site-specific slope-stability study.
Vieques, Culebra and Isla de Mona are not in the USGS model: no value. Puerto Rico's figure is the main island's.
An estimate from whole census blocks: rough for a barrio, where a class edge can cut a block.

Puerto Rico's share is over the main island's 3,275,833 residents in 2020 (11.5%); the Analysis tab's 'per 1,000 residents' view of the count divides it by all 3,285,874 residents of Puerto Rico, Vieques and Culebra included, as it does for every dataset, so it reads 114.4. The share is the figure to quote: Vieques and Culebra are not in the map, so their residents cannot be placed in a class.

facility_exposure.fx_road_flood_pct.plain: Out of every 100 km of main road in a municipio, how many run inside FEMA's 1% flood area.
facility_exposure.fx_road_flood_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 km de carretera principal de un municipio, cuántos pasan por el área de inundación de 1% de FEMA.
facility_exposure.fx_road_flood_pct.definition: The share of the kilometers of the municipio's main roads that run inside FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area. A road may be raised above it.
facility_exposure.fx_road_flood_pct.method: facility_exposure.py lays points and lines on FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area (the Special Flood Hazard Area of the observatory's flood layer, flood.geojson; the rule of the exposure series). It is an overlaid figure (decision 107): one published layer laid on another, with nothing assumed. The roads are the main roads of the traffic layer (traffic_roads.geojson: arterials and major collectors with a traffic count, FHWA HPMS). Each line is cut by the municipio outlines and each piece by the flood polygons it meets; lengths are measured in meters on a local flat projection.
facility_exposure.fx_road_flood_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 11.2%. Highest: Loíza (58.2%), Cataño (53.6%), Hormigueros (47.4%). A raised road or a bridge approach inside the area is counted like any other stretch.
caveats: It says where a building or a road stands, not that it floods: the floor height of a building and the height of a road are not known, and the flood layer is a simplified copy of FEMA's map.
FEMA's 1% area is the regulatory flood map: it does not include sea level rise, and some areas flood that it does not show.
facility_exposure.fx_road_flood_pct.source_detail: The observatory's own layers and files: flood.geojson (FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer), the facility layers, traffic_roads.geojson (FHWA HPMS) and the NCES school directory, https://educationdata.urban.org/api/v1/schools/ccd/directory/2024/?fips=72.

facility_exposure.fx_road_slr_pct.definition: The share of the kilometers of the municipio's main roads that run inside NOAA's area flooded by 3 ft of sea level rise above today's high tide (connected to the ocean), read every 20 m. A road may be raised above it.
facility_exposure.fx_road_slr_pct.method: facility_exposure.py lays points and lines on NOAA's extent of 3 ft of sea level rise above mean higher high water, connected to the ocean (the height the observatory's exposure series headline; low-lying areas not connected to the ocean are left out). Low-lying areas that 3 ft of sea level rise would leave cut off from the ocean are not counted.
Roads are read every 20 m, so a stretch shorter than that may be missed or counted whole.

caveats: It says what the ground under a building or road is rated, not that a slide will happen there; the map is not a substitute for a site-specific slope-stability study.

Read a low count as 'the building's own cell is not rated high', not as 'safe from slides': a slope above or below it, or the road to it, may be.
Vieques and Culebra are not in the USGS map: they have no value, and Puerto Rico's figure is of the main island.
2 points of the main island fall on a cell with no class (water or the edge of the map) and count as not high.
Roads are read every 20 m, so a stretch shorter than that may be missed or counted whole.

hazards.flood_zone.plain: The letter code that the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) gives a mapped flood area. A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE mean a 1% yearly chance of flooding (VE adds storm waves on the coast), and X and D mean lower or unstudied hazard.
hazards.flood_zone.plain_es: El código de letras que FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias) asigna a un área inundable en sus mapas. A, A99, AE, AH, AO y VE indican una probabilidad anual de inundación de 1% (VE suma el oleaje de tormenta en la costa), y X y D indican un riesgo menor o no estudiado.
hazards.flood_zone.definition: FLD_ZONE is the flood zone code of one map shape (polygon) in the National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). The NFHL is the digital version of FEMA's flood insurance rate maps. In the 2026-10 snapshot, this file holds eight codes for Puerto Rico: A, A99, AE, AH, AO, VE, X and D. Zones A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE form the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA): land FEMA maps with a 1% chance of flooding in any year (the '100-year flood'). Zone X has two parts, told apart by the ZONE_SUBTY field: a shaded 0.2% part (the '500-year flood') and an unshaded part of minimal hazard.
hazards.flood_zone.method: The build downloads layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones) of the NFHL for every record whose DFIRM_ID (the identifier of FEMA's Digital Flood Insurance Rate Map database) starts with 72, the Puerto Rico code. It publishes FLD_ZONE, ZONE_SUBTY and SFHA_TF. Outlines are simplified to about 5 m (0.00005 degrees) for display, and no polygon is dropped. The map layer draws the SFHA zones and zone X with the 0.2% subtype. It hides zone D and unshaded zone X.
hazards.flood_zone.how_to_read: Read the letters as families. VE is the coastal high-hazard zone, where waves add force to flooding. A, A99, AE, AH and AO are the other 1% zones. X with the 0.2% subtype is outside the 1% area but inside the wider 0.2% area. Unshaded X and D are not drawn on the observatory's maps. FEMA gives base flood elevations or depths for some zones, but the observatory does not publish them: the file holds only the zone, subtype and SFHA flag.
caveats: A zone is a map category. It is not a flood depth, a forecast or a record of damage in a past storm.
Zone D means FEMA has not studied the area. It does not mean low risk.
Unshaded X means minimal hazard on FEMA's map, not no hazard. Heavy rain can flood land that FEMA maps as minimal hazard.
FEMA publishes an effective date for each map panel. The observatory does not keep it, so the age of a polygon cannot be read from this file.

values.A: 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) where FEMA did not work out flood heights. Drawn on the maps. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 191 polygons.
values.A99: 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) that a federal flood-control system under construction is meant to protect once it is finished. Drawn. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 polygon.
values.AE: 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) where FEMA gives base flood elevations, the height the 1% flood is expected to reach. It is the most common SFHA zone. Drawn on the maps; floodway polygons are drawn red. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1,760 polygons, 138 of them also marked floodway. Zone X has more polygons overall (2,368).
values.AH: 1% yearly chance shallow flooding area (SFHA), usually ponding about 1 to 3 feet deep, with base flood elevations. Drawn. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 polygon.
values.AO: 1% yearly chance shallow flooding area (SFHA), usually water flowing over sloping ground about 1 to 3 feet deep, with flood depths given. Drawn; a floodway polygon is drawn red. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 25 polygons, 1 also marked floodway.
values.VE: Coastal 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) with an added hazard from storm waves, with base flood elevations. Drawn in the darkest blue, except a river floodway polygon, which is red. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 539 polygons, 1 of them a river floodway inside the coastal zone.
values.X: Outside the 1% area and not part of the SFHA. It has two parts, set by ZONE_SUBTY: 0.2% annual chance flood hazard (drawn light blue) and area of minimal flood hazard (not drawn). In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2,368 polygons, of which 1,648 are the 0.2% part and 720 the minimal-hazard part.
values.D: Possible but undetermined flood hazard: FEMA has not studied the area. Not part of the SFHA and not drawn. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 9 polygons.

hazards.flood_zone.geography: Puerto Rico. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file holds 4,894 polygons. 77 of the 78 municipios overlap a polygon in the 1% or 0.2% zones. Florida municipio lies wholly inside one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard). Coastal polygons extend over open water.
hazards.flood_zone.source_detail: FEMA NFHL MapServer layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones), DFIRM_ID LIKE '72%'. The zone meanings paraphrase FEMA's Flood Zones glossary page (fema.gov/glossary/flood-zones, updated 8 July 2020) and FEMA's FloodSmart page 'What is my flood zone' (floodsmart.gov), both read on 4 October 2026. Those pages give FEMA's own wording. The FEMA service itself carries no definition table. Cite as: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, Puerto Rico (DFIRM_ID beginning 72), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026 for observatory Snapshot 2026-10.

hazards.flood_subtype.plain: A second label from the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) that marks the 0.2% flood area, areas of minimal hazard and floodways. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is blank on 2,386 of the 4,894 polygons.
hazards.flood_subtype.plain_es: Una segunda etiqueta de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias) que marca el área de inundación de 0.2%, las áreas de riesgo mínimo y los cauces mayores (floodways). En el corte de datos de 2026-10 está en blanco en 2,386 de los 4,894 polígonos.
hazards.flood_subtype.definition: ZONE_SUBTY refines FLD_ZONE in FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL). It exists to separate the two kinds of zone X, which carry the same letter, and to mark floodways inside the 1% zones (the Special Flood Hazard Area, SFHA). In the 2026-10 snapshot this file holds four values. The field is blank (stored as null) for 2,386 polygons: the 1% zones that are not floodways, plus zone D.
hazards.flood_subtype.method: Copied from NFHL layer 28 without change. The observatory reads a subtype that contains '0.2' as the 0.2% zone, and one that contains 'FLOODWAY' as a floodway, drawn red.
hazards.flood_subtype.how_to_read: Use the subtype to tell the two kinds of zone X apart. In the observatory, only zone X with the 0.2% subtype counts as a flood zone. Unshaded X is ignored.
caveats: The wording is FEMA's. It can change between FEMA releases, and a later release can add other values. Only these four occur in the 2026-10 snapshot.

The observatory counts a zone X polygon as a flood zone only when its subtype contains '0.2'. A zone X polygon with any other subtype would be hidden and not flagged, even if FEMA draws it as a hazard. Only two X subtypes occur in the 2026-10 snapshot.
Blank is not an error. It is the normal value for a 1% polygon that is not a floodway.

values.0.2 PCT ANNUAL CHANCE FLOOD HAZARD: Zone X, shaded: moderate hazard, land between the limits of the 1% and the 0.2% ('500-year') floods. Drawn light blue. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1,648 polygons, all zone X, none in the SFHA.
values.AREA OF MINIMAL FLOOD HAZARD: Zone X, unshaded: land FEMA maps outside the 0.2% flood area. Not drawn and not counted as flood exposure. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 720 polygons, all zone X. Florida municipio lies wholly inside one of them.
values.FLOODWAY: Regulatory floodway: the river channel and the strip beside it that must stay clear so the 1% flood can pass without raising water levels by more than a set height. Always inside the SFHA. Drawn red. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 139 polygons (138 zone AE, 1 zone AO).
values.RIVERINE FLOODWAY SHOWN IN COASTAL ZONE: A river floodway that FEMA shows inside a coastal zone. Inside the SFHA. Drawn red like other floodways. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 polygon, zone VE.
values.null (blank): Stored as null in flood.geojson. No subtype given. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2,386 polygons, the A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE polygons that are not floodways (2,377) plus the 9 zone D polygons.

hazards.flood_zones_layer.plain: A map layer that shades the land the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) maps as flood-prone: the 1% zones, floodways, coastal high-hazard zones and the 0.2% zone. Zone D and unshaded X are left blank.
hazards.flood_zones_layer.plain_es: Una capa del mapa que sombrea los terrenos que FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias) identifica en sus mapas como propensos a inundación: las zonas de 1%, los cauces mayores, las zonas costeras de alto riesgo y la zona de 0.2%. La zona D y la zona X sin sombrear quedan en blanco.
hazards.flood_zones_layer.definition: The layer called 'Flood zones' (source FEMA, from its National Flood Hazard Layer, NFHL) in the 2D map and in the 3D view draws the polygons of flood.geojson that are in the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA) or are zone X with the 0.2% subtype. Red is a floodway. The darkest blue is a V zone (VE). Mid blue is any other SFHA zone (A, A99, AE, AH, AO). Light blue is the 0.2% zone. The layer hides zone D, unshaded X and the FEMA labels OPEN WATER and AREA NOT INCLUDED (neither occurs in the 2026-10 snapshot). Clicking a shaded area opens a popup with its zone and subtype, the same in the 2D map and the 3D view: one card with a section for each area under the click.
hazards.flood_zones_layer.method: Both maps draw the polygons in the SFHA and the zone X polygons whose subtype contains 0.2. They hide zone D, unshaded X and the two FEMA labels named above. Colors are red (floodway), darkest blue (V zones), mid blue (other SFHA zones) and light blue (0.2% zone), drawn at about 45% opacity. Place flags are not read from this file. They come from FEMA's unsimplified polygons.
hazards.flood_zones_layer.how_to_read: Color shows the zone family, not depth. Use the zone letter and subtype to read what FEMA says. An unshaded area is not proof of safety. The layer 'Flood zones' covers the 1% zones and the 0.2% zone. In the place and municipality figures, 'in a flood hazard area' means the 1% area only (the Special Flood Hazard Area).
caveats: Drawn outlines are simplified to about 5 m. A place at a zone edge can look inside or outside on the map while its flag uses FEMA's unsimplified outline.

hazards.flood_exposure_flag.plain: The observatory flags a tourism place as in a flood hazard area when its map point lies inside an area that the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) maps with a 1% chance of flooding each year. A second, wider flag also covers the area FEMA maps with a 0.2% chance. Places in areas that FEMA marks as minimal hazard, or has not studied, get neither flag.
hazards.flood_exposure_flag.plain_es: El observatorio marca un lugar turístico como dentro de una zona de riesgo de inundación cuando su punto en el mapa cae dentro de un área que FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias) identifica con una probabilidad de inundación de 1% cada año. Una segunda marca, más amplia, cubre también el área que FEMA identifica con una probabilidad de 0.2%. Los lugares en áreas que FEMA marca como de riesgo mínimo, o que no ha estudiado, no reciben ninguna de las dos marcas.
hazards.flood_exposure_flag.definition: For every place the build tests its coordinates against FEMA's flood polygons (point in polygon) and records two results. The sfha flag (Special Flood Hazard Area, SFHA) is yes when the point is inside a polygon where SFHA_TF is T. The flood zone value holds the zone and subtype when the point is in an SFHA polygon or in a zone X polygon with the 0.2% subtype. A point in unshaded X or zone D gets neither. If a point lies in more than one polygon, an SFHA polygon wins over a 0.2% polygon. Polygons labeled OPEN WATER or AREA NOT INCLUDED are skipped before testing (none occur in the 2026-10 snapshot).
hazards.flood_exposure_flag.method: The build tests each place's longitude and latitude with the 'within' test of Shapely (a Python geometry library) against FEMA's unsimplified polygons, not the simplified display file. A point exactly on an edge is not 'within'. Municipality counts use counted places only: confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship excluded. Percent in a flood hazard area is places in the SFHA divided by counted places, times 100, to one decimal.
hazards.flood_exposure_flag.how_to_read: 'In a flood hazard area' means the pin sits inside a polygon that FEMA maps with a 1% yearly chance of flooding. It does not say the place floods, how deep the water gets or whether the place has insurance.
caveats: Only the pin is tested. A building, beach or park can be partly inside a zone and partly outside.
The pin comes from Overture Maps and can be off the building by meters or more.
Coastal zones run along the shore, so shoreline places are flagged more often. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 428 of 817 counted beaches (52%) are in the SFHA, against 18% of all counted places.
No flag does not mean safe. Zone D and unshaded X are treated as not flagged, and FEMA's map covers only what FEMA studied.
Places of worship are flagged in the places file but left out of municipality percentages.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, Florida municipio lies wholly inside one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard), which is not flagged, so its 55 counted places show 0.0% in a flood hazard area. That is a mapped result, not missing data.
On a place, flood_zone X means the 0.2% zone. Unshaded X and zone D are never stored. A place with no flood_zone may still sit in unshaded X or outside FEMA's mapped area.
The percent is a share of listed places, not of land area, buildings or residents.
A municipio with few places can swing widely. See 'Tourism places in a flood hazard area (%)' for an example.
If a point sits in two polygons of the SFHA, the build keeps one of them and no rule decides which, so the zone letter can be either.

Municipality figures use the 24,209 counted places of that snapshot: tourism places with confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship excluded (see 'Which places each municipality count includes').

hazards.sfha.plain: A true or false flag on each polygon of the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) flood map. T means the polygon is in the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA), land with a 1% yearly chance of flooding, and F means it is not.
hazards.sfha.plain_es: Un indicador de verdadero o falso en cada polígono del mapa de inundación de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias). T significa que el polígono está en el Área Especial de Riesgo de Inundación (SFHA), terreno con una probabilidad anual de inundación de 1%, y F significa que no lo está.
hazards.sfha.definition: SFHA_TF holds the letter T (true) or F (false). The Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA) is the land FEMA maps as having a 1% chance of flooding in any year. T marks zones A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE. F marks every zone X and zone D polygon. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2,517 polygons are T and 2,377 are F.
hazards.sfha.method: Copied without change from layer 28 of FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL). The build sets a place's sfha flag to yes when the place falls in a polygon where SFHA_TF is T.
hazards.sfha.how_to_read: The observatory uses this flag, not the zone letter, to decide that a tourism place is in a flood hazard area. The route planner uses it too (see 'Share of the route in a flood hazard area').
caveats: F does not mean safe. Polygons in the 0.2% zone are F but can still flood.
The values are the text letters T and F, not true or false values.

values.T: In the Special Flood Hazard Area: zones A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2,517 polygons.
values.F: Not in the Special Flood Hazard Area. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2,377 polygons, made up of 1,648 shaded X, 720 unshaded X and 9 zone D.

hazards.flood_limits.plain: Zones from the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) describe the mapped flood hazard at a point on the map. They do not give a building's elevation, a flood depth for a given storm, or a place's insurance status.
hazards.flood_limits.plain_es: Las zonas de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias) describen el riesgo de inundación identificado en un punto del mapa. No dan la elevación de un edificio, la profundidad del agua en una tormenta dada ni la situación de seguro de un lugar.
hazards.flood_limits.definition: A FEMA flood zone is a regulatory map category for an area. It says how FEMA classes the chance of flooding there. It does not say how high a building's floor is, how deep water will be in a given storm, or what insurance a place has. The observatory holds no insurance data, so it cannot say whether a place needs or has flood insurance.
hazards.flood_limits.method: Applies to every FEMA-based figure in the observatory: the flood layers, a place's flood flag and the municipality percentages.
hazards.flood_limits.how_to_read: Treat the flags as a first screen. For a decision about a building, check the official FEMA flood map for that address and ask a qualified professional.
caveats: A 1% yearly chance is not 'once in 100 years'. Over 30 years the chance of at least one such flood is about 26%.
Zones come from studies of past and present conditions. They are not forecasts, and the observatory does not add sea level rise to them.
The flags are a point-in-polygon test on the pin (map point). They ignore ground elevation, drainage, flood-control works and building design.
FEMA's zones exist only where FEMA mapped. Zone D marks land that was not studied.

exposure.hu_flood.plain: How many housing units are in areas that FEMA maps as flood hazard areas, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
exposure.hu_flood.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda hay en zonas de riesgo de inundación según los mapas de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias), en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
exposure.hu_flood.definition: Two fields hold the count for each area. flood_sfha: the housing units of every census block whose internal point lies inside a Special Flood Hazard Area, the area FEMA maps as having a 1% chance of flooding in any year (the 100-year flood; zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99, V and VE). flood_any: the same for a block inside that area or inside the 0.2% annual chance (500-year) flood area. Both read site/data/flood.geojson. For the whole island, 172,281 housing units (10.8%) are in the first and 243,227 (15.2%) in the second, in the 2026-10 snapshot.
exposure.hu_flood.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 housing units up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). A polygon counts as the 1% area when FEMA's SFHA_TF field is T and as the 0.2% area when its subtype says so; unshaded zone X (minimal hazard), open water and unmapped areas are left out, as for tourism places. The outlines in flood.geojson are simplified by about 5 m; with FEMA's full-resolution outlines the island count for the 1% area changes by less than 0.3% (317,290 residents against 316,309).
exposure.hu_flood.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. A high share means many homes live where FEMA maps a flood hazard. It says nothing about the elevation, construction or insurance of a particular home.
caveats: A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
FEMA's maps show the hazard as mapped, with effective dates that differ by community. They are not a forecast, and a hazard FEMA has not mapped is not here.
Florida (72054) is mapped by FEMA entirely as minimal hazard, so its counts are zero: a result, not a gap.
A housing unit is a house, an apartment, a mobile home or a room meant as separate living quarters; people in group quarters (a dormitory, a nursing home) are not in housing units.

exposure.hu_low.plain: How many housing units live in low areas that NOAA says may flood with 1 to 10 feet of sea level rise but that its model does not connect to the ocean, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
exposure.hu_low.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda están en áreas bajas que, según NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica), podrían inundarse con un aumento del nivel del mar de 1 a 10 pies, pero que su modelo no conecta con el océano, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
exposure.hu_low.definition: Ten fields, low_1ft to low_10ft, hold the count for each area. NOAA also maps low-lying areas that lie at or below the water height for that many feet of sea level rise but that its model does not connect to the ocean (for example a hollow behind a road or a berm). NOAA says they may flood and shows them apart from the inundation. A field counts the housing units of every census block whose internal point lies inside such an area. An area leaves this set when a higher water level connects it to the ocean, so the count does not rise steadily with the height. Only 47 to 72 census blocks lie in these areas at any one height (build of 2026-10-06), so most areas have none and a count is the residents of a few blocks. For the whole island the most is 4,109 housing units (0.3%), at 7 ft.
exposure.hu_low.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 housing units up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). The layers PR_low_{n}ft are read the same way as the inundation layers; for the 3 ft layer the build was checked against GDAL's default: the same 68 blocks, no difference.
exposure.hu_low.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. Read it next to the connected area (exposure.hu_slr): a block is in one or the other, not both, at the same height (checked for all ten heights in the build of 2026-10-06: no block is in both).
caveats: Whether such an area floods depends on drainage, pumps and groundwater, which the data do not describe. NOAA does not count it as inundated.
The same screening-level limits as for the connected area apply: not a forecast, not for navigation, permitting or legal purposes.

exposure.hu_slr.plain: How many housing units live where NOAA's maps show the ocean flooding the land at high tide if the sea were 1 to 10 feet higher than today, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
exposure.hu_slr.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda están donde los mapas de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) muestran que el océano inundaría el terreno en marea alta si el mar estuviera de 1 a 10 pies más alto que hoy, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
exposure.hu_slr.definition: Ten fields, slr_1ft to slr_10ft, hold the count for each area. A field counts the housing units of every census block whose internal point lies inside NOAA's inundation polygon for that many feet of sea level rise above mean higher high water (the average of the higher high tide of each day), in water that is connected to the ocean. Each height includes the lower ones: the area flooded at 3 ft lies inside the area flooded at 4 ft. For the whole island: 7,143 housing units (0.4%) at 1 ft, 17,018 (1.1%) at 3 ft and 128,658 (8.1%) at 10 ft.
exposure.hu_slr.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 housing units up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). NOAA's polygons (the layers PR_slr_{n}ft of its Puerto Rico File Geodatabase) are read with GDAL's faster ring handling (OGR_ORGANIZE_POLYGONS=ONLY_CCW); the build was checked against GDAL's default, which takes minutes, on the 3 ft and 10 ft layers: the same blocks (1,392 and 3,936), no difference.
exposure.hu_slr.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. Each field is a number of feet above today's mean higher high water, not a year or a forecast: the 3D view turns a year and a NOAA 2022 scenario into the nearest whole foot from 1 to 10, and the same foot here gives the housing units in the flooded area on that map.
caveats: Exposed means living where the ground would be under water at high tide with that much sea level rise. It does not say that homes would be damaged or lost.

NOAA calls the data a screening-level tool. It uses a modified bathtub method that follows tides and hydrological connectivity, and does not include storm surge, rain, groundwater, erosion, subsidence or future construction. The vertical accuracy depends on the elevation data. NOAA's disclaimer says the maps show the scale of potential flooding, not exact locations, and are a planning reference, not for navigation, permitting or legal purposes.
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
A housing unit is a house, an apartment, a mobile home or a room meant as separate living quarters; people in group quarters (a dormitory, a nursing home) are not in housing units.

exposure.hu_surge.plain: How many housing units are where NOAA's maps show storm surge flooding the land in a category 1 to 5 hurricane (the near worst case, at high tide), counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
exposure.hu_surge.plain_es: Cuántas unidades de vivienda hay donde los mapas de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) muestran que la marejada ciclónica inundaría el terreno en un huracán de categoría 1 a 5 (casi el peor caso, en marea alta), en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
exposure.hu_surge.definition: Ten fields hold the count for each area. surge_cat1 to surge_cat5: the housing units of every census block whose internal point NOAA's storm surge map for a category 1 to 5 hurricane shows under water, at any depth. surge_deep_cat1 to surge_deep_cat5: the same, under 3 ft of water or more. For the whole island: 10,129 (0.6%) at category 1, 30,751 (1.9%) at category 3 and 73,273 (4.6%) at category 5; under 3 ft or more, 8,888 (0.6%) at category 3 and 32,683 (2.0%) at category 5.
exposure.hu_surge.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block), and adds its 2020 housing units up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree. For storm surge it reads the cell of NOAA's map under that point: a block counts at a category when the cell has any water, and in the deep field when the water is 3 ft or more above ground (band 4 and up; NHC's own map starts its second color at 3 ft). The cells are about 10 m. Every deep field lies inside its category's field, and the build checks it. The five categories are not strictly nested: each map is the highest water of its own set of model storms, and five block points in San Juan (247 residents, 124 housing units) are wet at category 4 and dry at category 5. The surge families were added on 2026-11-17 with python exposure.py --surge, which leaves every other family as it was. Check: every resident counted at category 1 is also inside FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area, which includes coastal surge; at category 3, 92.5%; at category 5, 63.0% (84.8% inside the 1% or 0.2% area).
exposure.hu_surge.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field). To get a share for a group of areas, add the counts and the totals first, then divide. Highest shares at category 3: Cataño 26.2%, Salinas 11.3%, Santa Isabel 11.3%; at category 5: Cataño 55.2%, Loíza 36.6%, Carolina 17.3%. 39 of the 78 municipios have none at category 5, most of them inland. Read the category as a what-if: the stronger the hurricane, the farther inland the water may reach.
caveats: Near worst case, not a forecast. Each category's map is NOAA's Maximum of MEOWs: the highest water at each place among many hypothetical storms of that category with different tracks, speeds and sizes, at high tide. No single storm floods all of it.

NOAA says the maps show the scale of potential flooding at a city or community level, not at a parcel or a single cell, and do not account for erosion, subsidence or future construction. Areas outside the SLOSH model's grids show no surge even where surge could reach.
Exposed means standing where the ground would be under water in that scenario. It does not say a home would be damaged: floor height and construction are not known.
These are not evacuation zones. Puerto Rico's evacuation zones are set by the emergency management bureau (NMEAD).
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that the edge of the surge cuts is counted in or out by its internal point.

hazards.storm_min_dist_km.plain: How close the storm's nearest recorded position came to the center of Puerto Rico, in kilometers. It is never more than 250.
hazards.storm_min_dist_km.plain_es: Cuán cerca del centro de Puerto Rico llegó la posición registrada más cercana de la tormenta, en kilómetros. Nunca es más de 250.
hazards.storm_min_dist_km.definition: min_dist_km is the smallest great-circle distance between any best-track position of the storm and the point 18.22 N, 66.45 W, rounded to a whole kilometer. The distance uses an Earth radius of 6,371 km. In the 2026-10 snapshot, values run from 6 to 250.
hazards.storm_min_dist_km.method: Haversine distance from every track position to the center point, minimum, then rounded.
hazards.storm_min_dist_km.how_to_read: A small value means the storm passed near the middle of the island. A value of 100 km can still mean a coastline close to the storm, because the main island is about 180 km long from west to east.
caveats: It is measured to the center point, not to the coast, and not to Vieques, Culebra or Mona.
Positions are 6 hours apart. The true closest distance may be smaller.
A value of 6 km does not mean the eye passed over land. Positions are rounded to 0.1 degree, about 11 km.

hazards.storm_selection.plain: The observatory keeps every Atlantic storm from 1851 to 2025 that had a recorded position within 250 km (155 miles) of the center of Puerto Rico. The storms come from the Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2) of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). In the 2026-10 snapshot that is 157 storms.
hazards.storm_selection.plain_es: El observatorio conserva toda tormenta del Atlántico de 1851 a 2025 que tuvo una posición registrada a 250 km (155 millas) o menos del centro de Puerto Rico. Las tormentas provienen de la Base de Datos de Huracanes, 2.ª generación (HURDAT2) de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica). En el corte de datos de 2026-10 son 157 tormentas.
hazards.storm_selection.definition: The National Hurricane Center (NHC), part of NOAA, publishes HURDAT2, the Atlantic hurricane database: a list of storms, each with positions and winds every 6 hours. The build measures the distance from each best-track position to a fixed point at 18.22 N, 66.45 W, near the middle of the main island. A storm is kept when its closest position is 250 km (about 155 miles) or less from that point. Each kept storm carries four derived values: min_dist_km, max_wind, wind_near_pr and cat_near_pr.
hazards.storm_selection.method: 1) Read the HURDAT2 Atlantic file (hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt): one header line per storm (id, name), then one row per position (date, time, status, latitude, longitude, wind in knots). 2) Keep every row of a kept storm as its track, so the track covers the storm's whole life. 3) min_dist_km is the smallest great-circle (haversine) distance from any position to the center point, rounded to a whole km. Keep the storm when the unrounded value is 250 km or less. 4) max_wind is the largest wind on the whole track. 5) wind_near_pr is the largest wind among positions within 250 km of the center point. 6) cat_near_pr is the Saffir-Simpson category of wind_near_pr, with 0 for winds below 64 knots. 7) Sort storms by the time of their first position. meta.json records the count and the year range.
hazards.storm_selection.how_to_read: 250 km is measured from one point, not from the coast. Along the compass lines through that point, the circle reaches about 160 km beyond the east coast, 175 km beyond the west coast and 220 km beyond the north and south coasts. A storm on the list may never have touched land.
caveats: The test uses best-track positions, not the line between them. A fast storm could cross the circle between two positions and be left out.
Only Atlantic storms (id prefix AL) are read. Eastern Pacific storms are not included.

Observation methods changed a great deal between 1851 and 2025. Older tracks and winds are less certain, so counts by decade should not be read as a trend. In the 2026-10 snapshot the 2020s have six years (2020 to 2025), so that decade is incomplete.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 157 storms are kept, and 65 had hurricane-strength wind (category 1 or higher) near the island by this method.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 157 include 6 systems that were only a low, disturbance or tropical wave when within 250 km, and 22 storms with a single position inside the circle. The count is storms that came near, not storms that struck the island.

hazards.storm_layer.plain: A 3D map layer that draws the path of storms near Puerto Rico since 1851, colored by category near the island. At first it shows only category 3 and higher; you can filter by years and strength and play it through time.
hazards.storm_layer.plain_es: Una capa del mapa 3D que traza la ruta de las tormentas cerca de Puerto Rico desde 1851, con colores según su categoría cerca de la isla. Al principio muestra solo la categoría 3 o más; se puede filtrar por años y por fuerza, y reproducir en el tiempo.
hazards.storm_layer.definition: The layer 'Storm tracks within 250 km' draws each storm's track as a line and each recorded position as a dot. Line color is cat_near_pr. Line width is 1.5 pixels plus the category. Dot color follows each point's own wind with the same thresholds, and dot size grows with that wind. Hovering a line shows the name, year, category, peak wind near the island and closest distance. A list shows the 25 strongest storms in the window.
hazards.storm_layer.method: Filters: a year window (1851 to 2025 by default) and a minimum category (the menu's All (incl. tropical storms), Hurricane (Cat 1+), Major (Cat 3+) and Cat 4+; the default is Major (Cat 3+)). In the Storms mode of the time bar, and when you press Play through the years, the layer shows storms from the current year and the 10 years before it (11 calendar years) and fades older ones, down to 15% opacity. The 25-storm list sorts by category, then wind near the island, then newest year.
hazards.storm_layer.how_to_read: Thicker lines mean a stronger storm near the island. Color follows the category: gray 0, blue 1, green 2, orange 3, red 4, dark red 5. A line may extend far beyond Puerto Rico, because the whole track is drawn. When you switch the layer on, it shows only category 3 and higher storms (29 of the 157 in the 2026-10 snapshot). Choose All (incl. tropical storms) to see every storm in the file.
caveats: Lines join recorded positions with straight segments.
The 3D hover tip labels every category 0 storm 'Tropical storm', and the list badge shows TS (tropical storm), although some had only depression-strength winds near the island.
There is no Category 2+ option in the minimum-category filter.

hazards.storm_limits.plain: The Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2) of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is a best-track record. It is revised after each season, shows the storm's own wind and position, and says nothing about rain, surge, damage or deaths.
hazards.storm_limits.plain_es: La Base de Datos de Huracanes, 2.ª generación (HURDAT2) de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) es un registro de mejor trayectoria. Se revisa después de cada temporada, muestra el viento y la posición de la propia tormenta, y no dice nada sobre lluvia, marejada ciclónica, daños ni muertes.
hazards.storm_limits.definition: A best track is a final estimate of a storm's position and wind. National Hurricane Center (NHC) specialists build it after the season ends, from all the observations. NHC revises it after each season and sometimes re-analyses older storms. The observatory uses one release, covering 1851 to 2025. A newer release is used only when the observatory is rebuilt to use it.
hazards.storm_limits.method: Applies to every storm value in the observatory: id, name, year, track, max_wind, wind_near_pr, cat_near_pr and min_dist_km.
hazards.storm_limits.how_to_read: Use the data to see which storms came near the island and how strong they were while near. Do not use it to say how much damage a storm did.
caveats: The file runs through the 2025 season (NHC file updated 23 September 2026). Storms after the 2025 season are not in the 2026-10 snapshot. NHC also revised some 1971 to 1975 storms in that file, so a few older values differ from earlier snapshots (for example, Eloise 1975 now peaks at 55 knots near the island, so it is category 0, not 1).
HURDAT2 holds no rainfall, storm surge, damage or death figures. The observatory keeps only time, position, wind and status. It drops central pressure and wind-radius columns.
Winds are sustained one-minute averages in 5-knot steps. They are not gusts.
Older storms are less certain, and some storms may be missing from the early record.
Storm names repeat. Use the id.

hazards.storm_wind_near_pr.plain: The highest sustained wind of the storm, in knots, among its best-track positions within 250 km of the center of Puerto Rico.
hazards.storm_wind_near_pr.plain_es: El viento sostenido más alto de la tormenta, en nudos, entre sus posiciones de mejor trayectoria a 250 km o menos del centro de Puerto Rico.
hazards.storm_wind_near_pr.definition: wind_near_pr is the largest 'maximum sustained wind' (one-minute average, in knots) among the storm's positions that lie within 250 km of the point 18.22 N, 66.45 W. In the 2026-10 snapshot, values run from 25 to 155 knots, in steps of 5. A knot is 1.15 miles per hour. The category value cat_near_pr is worked out from it.
hazards.storm_wind_near_pr.method: Filter the track to positions with a wind value and a distance of 250 km or less from the center point, then take the maximum wind.
hazards.storm_wind_near_pr.how_to_read: It is the storm's own wind at a position near the island. It is not a wind measured on land or in a town.
caveats: The position can be as far as 250 km away. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Maria (2017) shows 150 knots from a position about 212 km from the center. Its best-track winds were 135 knots at 63 km and 115 knots at 26 km.
Positions are 6 hours apart, so the true peak between two positions may be higher or lower.

hazards.storm_max_wind.plain: The best estimate by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) of the storm's highest sustained wind anywhere along its whole track, in knots. It is not the wind that reached Puerto Rico.
hazards.storm_max_wind.plain_es: El mejor estimado de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) del viento sostenido más alto de la tormenta en cualquier punto de toda su trayectoria, en nudos. No es el viento que llegó a Puerto Rico.
hazards.storm_max_wind.definition: max_wind is the largest value of the 'maximum sustained wind' (the wind averaged over one minute near the surface) among all best-track positions of the storm. It is in knots. One knot is 1.15 miles per hour or 1.85 km per hour. In the 2026-10 snapshot, values run from 30 to 160 knots, in steps of 5.
hazards.storm_max_wind.method: The maximum of the wind column over every row of the storm, ignoring rows with no wind value. In the 2026-10 snapshot every row has a wind value.
hazards.storm_max_wind.how_to_read: Compare it with wind_near_pr. If the two differ, the storm was stronger somewhere else. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Dorian (2019) peaked at 160 knots far from the island, but its highest wind within 250 km was 75 knots.
caveats: The peak can occur thousands of kilometers from Puerto Rico.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 156 values are multiples of 5 knots, which is how HURDAT2 reports wind.
It is a sustained wind, not a gust.

hazards.storm_cat_near_pr.plain: The storm's hurricane category, 1 to 5, based on its peak wind while within 250 km of the center of Puerto Rico. 0 means below hurricane strength.
hazards.storm_cat_near_pr.plain_es: La categoría de huracán de la tormenta, de 1 a 5, según su viento máximo mientras estuvo a 250 km o menos del centro de Puerto Rico. 0 significa que no llegó a fuerza de huracán.
hazards.storm_cat_near_pr.definition: cat_near_pr is the Saffir-Simpson category of wind_near_pr, using the wind thresholds in knots: 137 or more is 5, 113 to 136 is 4, 96 to 112 is 3, 83 to 95 is 2, 64 to 82 is 1, and below 64 is 0. Counts in the 2026-10 snapshot: category 0, 92; 1, 21; 2, 15; 3, 16; 4, 8; 5, 5. 29 storms are category 3 or higher (major).
hazards.storm_cat_near_pr.method: A chain of thresholds on wind_near_pr. The same thresholds color the storm tracks in the 3D view and drive its minimum-category filter (the menu's All (incl. tropical storms), Hurricane (Cat 1+), Major (Cat 3+) and Cat 4+).
hazards.storm_cat_near_pr.how_to_read: Use it to compare how strong storms were while near the island. It is not the category at landfall.
caveats: Category 0 is not a Saffir-Simpson category. It groups storms below hurricane strength. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 21 of the 92 have winds under 34 knots (tropical depression strength or weaker) and 71 have 34 to 63 knots (tropical storm strength). The 3D hover tip labels every category 0 storm 'Tropical storm', and the list badge shows TS (tropical storm), although some had only depression-strength winds near the island.

The value uses any position within 250 km, whatever its status code. In the 2026-10 snapshot those positions are hurricane (205), tropical storm (204), tropical depression (50), low (8), disturbance (5), subtropical storm (4) and tropical wave (2). No extratropical position is within 250 km.
The scale rates wind only. It does not rate rain, storm surge or flooding, which caused much of the harm in many storms.

Category 4 and 5 here often come from a position far from the island. In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 13 storms in categories 4 and 5 had a peak-wind position 155 km or more from the center. The unnamed 1928 storm also recorded its peak wind (140 knots) 63 km away. Do not read the category counts as hits on the island.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, Maria (2017) shows category 5 here because of a 150-knot position about 212 km away. Its best-track winds were 135 knots at 63 km and 115 knots at 26 km.

hazards.hurricane_scale.plain: The scale that sorts hurricanes by sustained wind, from category 1 to 5. The observatory adds category 0 for storms below hurricane strength.
hazards.hurricane_scale.plain_es: La escala que clasifica los huracanes por su viento sostenido, de la categoría 1 a la 5. El observatorio agrega la categoría 0 para las tormentas que no llegan a fuerza de huracán.
hazards.hurricane_scale.definition: The Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale rates a hurricane by its maximum sustained wind. The observatory applies it in knots to wind_near_pr. It rates wind only. It does not rate rain, storm surge or flooding. Categories 3, 4 and 5 are 'major' hurricanes.
hazards.hurricane_scale.method: The observatory applies the thresholds 64, 83, 96, 113 and 137 knots when it works out each storm's category and when the 3D view colors each point by its own wind.
hazards.hurricane_scale.how_to_read: Colors in the 3D view run from gray (category 0) through blue, green, orange and red to dark red (category 5).
caveats: Category 0 is added by the observatory and is not part of the official scale.

AL152017 es la tormenta del Atlántico número 15 de 2017.
hazards.storm_id.definition: id holds the HURDAT2 storm identifier: the basin code AL (Atlantic), a two-digit storm number within the year, and the four-digit year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 156 ids start with AL and are different. It is the only reliable key, because names repeat (two storms are named Earl, in 2010 and 2022) and 85 storms have no name.
hazards.storm_id.method: Copied from the HURDAT2 header line of each storm.
hazards.storm_id.how_to_read: Use id to find or cite one storm. The last four characters are its year.
caveats: The number is the storm's position in that year's list. It does not say how strong the storm was.

En el corte de datos de 2026-10, 85 de las 157 tormentas no tienen nombre; la última es de 1981.

hazards.storm_name.how_to_read: Names repeat across years. Always pair a name with its year, or use the id.
caveats: A name is a label for the storm, not a measure of its strength.

hazards.storm_track.plain: The list of best-track positions of the storm, from its first record to its last. Each point has longitude, latitude, time, wind in knots and a status code.
hazards.storm_track.plain_es: La lista de posiciones de mejor trayectoria de la tormenta, desde su primer registro hasta el último. Cada punto tiene longitud, latitud, hora, viento en nudos y un código de estado.
hazards.storm_track.definition: track is a list of points. Each point is five values: [longitude, latitude, time, wind, status]. Longitude is in degrees (negative is west). Latitude is in degrees north. Time is text in the form YYYYMMDDHHMM, in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), as the format of the National Hurricane Center (NHC) specifies. Wind is the maximum sustained wind in knots. Status is a code from the Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2). In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 157 tracks hold 6,624 points, from 1 to 133 per storm. Most points are at 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC. 189 are at other times, such as landfall or peak intensity.
hazards.storm_track.method: Every row of the storm is kept, so the track covers the storm's whole life and not only the part within 250 km. Positions are rounded to 0.01 degree (HURDAT2 gives 0.1 degree). HURDAT2's record identifier (for example L for landfall), pressure and wind-radius columns are not kept. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 478 of the points lie within 250 km of the center point.
hazards.storm_track.how_to_read: The 3D map joins the points with straight lines. The real path curves between them. Point size and color follow each point's own wind.
caveats: Winds are in 5-knot steps and positions in 0.1 degree. These are best estimates, not exact measurements.
Early records rely on ships and land stations, so older tracks are less certain.

exposure.pop_flood.plain: How many residents are in areas that FEMA maps as flood hazard areas, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
exposure.pop_flood.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes hay en zonas de riesgo de inundación según los mapas de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias), en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
exposure.pop_flood.definition: Two fields hold the count for each area. flood_sfha: the residents of every census block whose internal point lies inside a Special Flood Hazard Area, the area FEMA maps as having a 1% chance of flooding in any year (the 100-year flood; zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99, V and VE). flood_any: the same for a block inside that area or inside the 0.2% annual chance (500-year) flood area. Both read site/data/flood.geojson. For the whole island, 316,309 residents (9.6%) are in the first and 454,706 (13.8%) in the second, in the 2026-10 snapshot.
exposure.pop_flood.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 residents up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). A polygon counts as the 1% area when FEMA's SFHA_TF field is T and as the 0.2% area when its subtype says so; unshaded zone X (minimal hazard), open water and unmapped areas are left out, as for tourism places. The outlines in flood.geojson are simplified by about 5 m; with FEMA's full-resolution outlines the island count for the 1% area changes by less than 0.3% (317,290 residents against 316,309).
exposure.pop_flood.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. A high share means many people live where FEMA maps a flood hazard. It says nothing about the elevation, construction or insurance of a particular home.
caveats: A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.
FEMA's maps show the hazard as mapped, with effective dates that differ by community. They are not a forecast, and a hazard FEMA has not mapped is not here.
Florida (72054) is mapped by FEMA entirely as minimal hazard, so its counts are zero: a result, not a gap.
exposure.pop_flood.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

exposure.pop_low.plain: How many residents live in low areas that NOAA says may flood with 1 to 10 feet of sea level rise but that its model does not connect to the ocean, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
exposure.pop_low.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes viven en áreas bajas que, según NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica), podrían inundarse con un aumento del nivel del mar de 1 a 10 pies, pero que su modelo no conecta con el océano, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
exposure.pop_low.definition: Ten fields, low_1ft to low_10ft, hold the count for each area. NOAA also maps low-lying areas that lie at or below the water height for that many feet of sea level rise but that its model does not connect to the ocean (for example a hollow behind a road or a berm). NOAA says they may flood and shows them apart from the inundation. A field counts the residents of every census block whose internal point lies inside such an area. An area leaves this set when a higher water level connects it to the ocean, so the count does not rise steadily with the height. Only 47 to 72 census blocks lie in these areas at any one height (build of 2026-10-06), so most areas have none and a count is the residents of a few blocks. For the whole island the most is 7,148 residents (0.2%), at 7 ft.
exposure.pop_low.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 residents up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). The layers PR_low_{n}ft are read the same way as the inundation layers; for the 3 ft layer the build was checked against GDAL's default: the same 68 blocks, no difference.
exposure.pop_low.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. Read it next to the connected area (exposure.pop_slr): a block is in one or the other, not both, at the same height (checked for all ten heights in the build of 2026-10-06: no block is in both).
caveats: Whether such an area floods depends on drainage, pumps and groundwater, which the data do not describe. NOAA does not count it as inundated.
The same screening-level limits as for the connected area apply: not a forecast, not for navigation, permitting or legal purposes.
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.

exposure.pop_slr.plain: How many residents live where NOAA's maps show the ocean flooding the land at high tide if the sea were 1 to 10 feet higher than today, counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
exposure.pop_slr.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes viven donde los mapas de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) muestran que el océano inundaría el terreno en marea alta si el mar estuviera de 1 a 10 pies más alto que hoy, en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
exposure.pop_slr.definition: Ten fields, slr_1ft to slr_10ft, hold the count for each area. A field counts the residents of every census block whose internal point lies inside NOAA's inundation polygon for that many feet of sea level rise above mean higher high water (the average of the higher high tide of each day), in water that is connected to the ocean. Each height includes the lower ones: the area flooded at 3 ft lies inside the area flooded at 4 ft. For the whole island: 11,005 residents (0.3%) at 1 ft, 25,302 (0.8%) at 3 ft and 213,681 (6.5%) at 10 ft.
exposure.pop_slr.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block): inside the polygons of a layer, or within 400 m of a stop. It adds the block's 2020 residents up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree and counts add up exactly between levels. It writes nothing unless every area's total equals the crosswalk's and every set lies inside its superset (the area flooded at 2 ft is inside the area flooded at 3 ft; a stop with a current timetable is a stop). NOAA's polygons (the layers PR_slr_{n}ft of its Puerto Rico File Geodatabase) are read with GDAL's faster ring handling (OGR_ORGANIZE_POLYGONS=ONLY_CCW); the build was checked against GDAL's default, which takes minutes, on the 3 ft and 10 ft layers: the same blocks (1,392 and 3,936), no difference.
exposure.pop_slr.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field), which puts a small barrio and a large municipio on one scale. To get a share for a group of areas (the island, a region), add the counts and the totals first, then divide; do not average the shares. Each field is a number of feet above today's mean higher high water, not a year or a forecast: the 3D view turns a year and a NOAA 2022 scenario into the nearest whole foot from 1 to 10, and the same foot here gives the residents in the flooded area on that map.
caveats: Exposed means living where the ground would be under water at high tide with that much sea level rise. It does not say that homes would be damaged or lost.

NOAA calls the data a screening-level tool. It uses a modified bathtub method that follows tides and hydrological connectivity, and does not include storm surge, rain, groundwater, erosion, subsidence or future construction. The vertical accuracy depends on the elevation data. NOAA's disclaimer says the maps show the scale of potential flooding, not exact locations, and are a planning reference, not for navigation, permitting or legal purposes.
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that a boundary cuts is counted in or out by its internal point: near an edge the count can be higher or lower than the true number.

exposure.pop_surge.plain: How many residents are where NOAA's maps show storm surge flooding the land in a category 1 to 5 hurricane (the near worst case, at high tide), counted for each municipio, barrio and census tract.
exposure.pop_surge.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes hay donde los mapas de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) muestran que la marejada ciclónica inundaría el terreno en un huracán de categoría 1 a 5 (casi el peor caso, en marea alta), en cada municipio, barrio y sector censal.
exposure.pop_surge.definition: Ten fields hold the count for each area. surge_cat1 to surge_cat5: the residents of every census block whose internal point NOAA's storm surge map for a category 1 to 5 hurricane shows under water, at any depth. surge_deep_cat1 to surge_deep_cat5: the same, under 3 ft of water or more. For the whole island: 15,961 (0.5%) at category 1, 46,689 (1.4%) at category 3 and 120,934 (3.7%) at category 5; under 3 ft or more, 14,025 (0.4%) at category 3 and 50,353 (1.5%) at category 5.
exposure.pop_surge.method: exposure.py counts each 2020 Census block whole, by its internal point (the Census Bureau's point that always lies inside the block), and adds its 2020 residents up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold it, so the three files agree. For storm surge it reads the cell of NOAA's map under that point: a block counts at a category when the cell has any water, and in the deep field when the water is 3 ft or more above ground (band 4 and up; NHC's own map starts its second color at 3 ft). The cells are about 10 m. Every deep field lies inside its category's field, and the build checks it. The five categories are not strictly nested: each map is the highest water of its own set of model storms, and five block points in San Juan (247 residents, 124 housing units) are wet at category 4 and dry at category 5. The surge families were added on 2026-11-17 with python exposure.py --surge, which leaves every other family as it was. Check: every resident counted at category 1 is also inside FEMA's 1% annual chance flood area, which includes coastal surge; at category 3, 92.5%; at category 5, 63.0% (84.8% inside the 1% or 0.2% area).
exposure.pop_surge.how_to_read: Compare areas by share: divide a count by the area's total (the total field). To get a share for a group of areas, add the counts and the totals first, then divide. Highest shares at category 3: Cataño 21.8%, Santa Isabel 10.2%, Loíza 9.2%; at category 5: Cataño 52.3%, Loíza 36.4%, Carolina 15.0%. 39 of the 78 municipios have none at category 5, most of them inland. Read the category as a what-if: the stronger the hurricane, the farther inland the water may reach.
caveats: Near worst case, not a forecast. Each category's map is NOAA's Maximum of MEOWs: the highest water at each place among many hypothetical storms of that category with different tracks, speeds and sizes, at high tide. No single storm floods all of it.

NOAA says the maps show the scale of potential flooding at a city or community level, not at a parcel or a single cell, and do not account for erosion, subsidence or future construction. Areas outside the SLOSH model's grids show no surge even where surge could reach.
Exposed means living where the ground would be under water in that scenario. It does not say a home would be damaged: floor height and construction are not known.
These are not evacuation zones. Puerto Rico's evacuation zones are set by the emergency management bureau (NMEAD).
A census block is counted whole by one point, so a block that the edge of the surge cuts is counted in or out by its internal point.
