hazards.slr_year_to_feet.plain: The 3D view picks a layer of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) from a year and a scenario. It reads the scenario's rise in meters for that year, converts it to feet, rounds to a whole foot and keeps it between 1 and 10.
hazards.slr_year_to_feet.plain_es: La vista 3D escoge una capa de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) a partir de un año y un escenario. Lee el aumento del nivel del mar del escenario en metros para ese año, lo convierte a pies, lo redondea a un pie entero y lo mantiene entre 1 y 10.
hazards.slr_year_to_feet.definition: In the Time tab of the 3D view, you choose a year (2020 to 2150, in steps of 5) and one of four NOAA 2022 scenarios. The page holds a small table of global mean sea level rise, in meters above the year-2000 level, for 2020, 2050, 2100 and 2150 in each scenario. It joins those points with straight lines, multiplies the meters by 3.28084 to get feet, rounds to the nearest whole foot and limits the result to 1 to 10 ft. It then loads NOAA's layer for that number of feet.
hazards.slr_year_to_feet.method: For a year y between two table years y0 and y1, the page works out: meters = m0 + (m1 - m0) x (y - y0) / (y1 - y0). Feet = meters x 3.28084, rounded half up, then at least 1 and at most 10. The 2D map has no year. Its slider sets the feet directly.
hazards.slr_year_to_feet.how_to_read: Several years show the same layer, because the result is rounded to whole feet. The layer is 1 ft from 2020 until 2050 in High and Intermediate-High, until 2060 in Intermediate and until 2090 in Intermediate-Low. A year on the slider is a position on a scenario curve, not a prediction that the sea will reach that level in that year. The Year slider opens at 2050 and the scenario at Intermediate, which gives the 1 ft layer.
caveats: The curves are global averages typed into the page code. They are not Puerto Rico local values.
The scenarios measure rise above the year-2000 sea level. The NOAA layers show water above today's mean higher high water. The observatory treats the two as the same number of feet.
Only four scenarios are offered: Intermediate-Low, Intermediate, Intermediate-High and High. NOAA's 2022 report also has a Low scenario, which the observatory does not offer.
The result is capped at 10 ft, so the High scenario in 2150 (12.8 ft) shows the 10 ft layer.

The layer is never lower than 1 ft. In 2020 the table value is 0.07 m (0.2 ft) in every scenario, so the 1 ft layer shows more water than the table gives. The floor changes the result only while the table value is under 0.5 ft: up to 2025 in High and Intermediate-High, and up to 2030 in Intermediate and Intermediate-Low.
These meters are the observatory's own approximate readings of NOAA's tables, not NOAA's published numbers. For scenario values to cite, use the NOAA report.

hazards.slr_inundation.plain: Map tiles streamed live from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) that show land that would be under water at high tide if the sea rose by 1 to 10 feet. The observatory does not store them.
hazards.slr_inundation.plain_es: Mosaicos de mapa que se transmiten en vivo desde NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) y que muestran los terrenos que quedarían bajo agua en marea alta si el mar subiera de 1 a 10 pies. El observatorio no los guarda.
hazards.slr_inundation.definition: Each tile layer shows the area that NOAA's Office for Coastal Management maps as flooded when sea level is a set number of feet above today's mean higher high water (MHHW), the average height of the higher of the two daily high tides. The observatory offers whole-foot steps from 1 to 10 ft. NOAA draws the tiles. The browser asks coast.noaa.gov for them while the layer is on. No sea level data are kept in the observatory's data files.
hazards.slr_inundation.method: NOAA draws the tiles. While the layer is on, the browser asks https://coast.noaa.gov/arcgis/rest/services/dc_slr/slr_{N}ft/MapServer for tiles, where N is the height in feet. Tiles are requested up to zoom level 16 and enlarged beyond that. If NOAA does not answer, the page shows a message. For the controls, see 'Sea level rise switch and slider (2D map)', '3D view: Sea level by year' and '3D view: flood zones and sea level switches'.
hazards.slr_inundation.how_to_read: Tinted areas are where NOAA maps flooding at the chosen height above mean higher high water, at the highest regular high tides. It is a what-if for planning, not a forecast for a year. NOAA says all features should be verified with a site visit. To cite a layer, give the feet value and the date you viewed it, because NOAA can update the service.
caveats: NOAA describes the layers as a screening-level tool. They show the scale of possible flooding, not exact locations.
NOAA says the layers do not account for erosion, subsidence or future construction.
NOAA says the layers show water at the highest high tides and exclude wind-driven tides. Its viewer does not model storm surge.

As of 4 October 2026, NOAA's service for the 3 ft layer holds two sublayers, 'Low-lying Areas' and 'Depth', and the observatory shows NOAA's full tile set. NOAA's Sea Level Rise Viewer help explains how NOAA defines low-lying areas. Read it before concluding that a particular place would flood.
NOAA provides the data as is, for planning and not for permits or navigation.
The observatory keeps no copy. If NOAA changes or removes the service, the layer stops working.

svi.svi_overall.plain: How socially vulnerable each municipio is, as CDC ranks it among the 78 municipios: 0 is the least vulnerable and 1 the most.
svi.svi_overall.plain_es: Cuán vulnerable socialmente es cada municipio, según el rango de los CDC entre los 78 municipios: 0 es el menos vulnerable y 1 el más vulnerable.
svi.svi_overall.definition: CDC's overall rank, from the four themes together: socioeconomic status, household characteristics, racial and ethnic minority status, and housing type and transportation (16 survey measures). A rank of 0 is the least vulnerable municipio and 1 the most vulnerable, among the 78 municipios of Puerto Rico only: it cannot be compared with a state's.
svi.svi_overall.method: svi.py reads CDC's two Puerto Rico files of the Social Vulnerability Index 2022 (counties and census tracts) and keeps CDC's percentile rank as published. CDC ranks each area on 16 measures of the American Community Survey 2018-2022, adds the ranks within each of four themes, ranks the sums, and does the same across themes for the overall rank. Puerto Rico is ranked apart from the states: a municipio among the 78 municipios, a tract among Puerto Rico's tracts. CDC's no-value code (-999) becomes an empty value, never a zero. Nothing is recomputed.
svi.svi_overall.how_to_read: Most vulnerable municipios on this rank: Loíza (1.00), Ponce (0.99) and Salinas (0.97). Least: Guaynabo (0.00), Camuy (0.01) and Dorado (0.03). The tract file has a value for 919 of the 981 census tracts.
caveats: The overall rank includes CDC's third theme, racial and ethnic minority status, which cannot tell places apart in Puerto Rico: its largest rank among Puerto Rico's tracts is 0.5223, because in 897 of the 922 tracts with a value 95% or more of the residents are a minority by the national definition.. The observatory does not publish that theme as a dataset.
FPR's own WCRP vulnerability indicators (wcrp.html) rank barrios with a different method and more local inputs: the two are not the same index.
It is a rank, not an amount: 0.80 means more vulnerable than 80% of Puerto Rico's municipios (or tracts), not 80% vulnerable. Do not add or average ranks.
Ranked within Puerto Rico only. A value cannot be compared with a state's, and a municipio's rank is not the average of its tracts' ranks.
The measures are survey estimates of 2018-2022 with margins of error; CDC publishes no margin for the rank itself. Small differences between ranks mean little.

storm_recovery.storm_months_back.plain: How many months after Hurricanes María (2017) and Fiona (2022) the area's night-time light came back to near what it was the year before.
storm_recovery.storm_months_back.plain_es: Cuántos meses después de los huracanes María (2017) y Fiona (2022) la luz nocturna del área volvió a acercarse a la del año anterior.
storm_recovery.storm_months_back.definition: The months from the hurricane's month (September) until the area's night-time light was back to at least 80% of the same month the year before, two months in a row. 1 means back by October. The year 2017 is Hurricane María (with Irma earlier that month); 2022 is Hurricane Fiona. Each month after the storm is compared with the same month in the twelve months before the storm month (September to August). Light counts as back in the first month after September when it and the next month are both at least 80% of the same month the year before; the figure counts months from September (1 means back by October). Areas with a mean under 0.5 nW/cm²/sr in the year before are too dim to read and have no figure. Light is a proxy for power and activity, not a count of homes with power. It can stay lower after a storm because homes were left empty, businesses closed or streetlights were changed to LED (whiter light, which the sensor sees less of), and a month is a composite of its clear nights, so an outage shorter than a few weeks barely shows. The rule is the observatory's; the island's figures agree with the utility's record of customers restored (docs/storm_recovery.md).
storm_recovery.storm_months_back.method: storm_recovery.py reads the observatory's monthly night-time light (nightlights_monthly.json: NASA Black Marble VNP46A3, pixels of about 460 m pooled by barrio, municipio and Puerto Rico) and compares each month after the storm month (September) with the same calendar month in the twelve months before it, so that cloudy and clear seasons cancel out. Light counts as back in the first month when it and the next month are both at least 80% of the same month the year before; the figure counts months from September. The lowest month is the darkest from September to March, as a share of the same month the year before. An area whose mean in the year before is under 0.5 nW/cm²/sr has no figure: its light moves 20% to 70% from month to month without any storm. No network and no key: the file is rebuilt with the night-light file.
storm_recovery.storm_months_back.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 8 months after María (back by 2018-05), 1 after Fiona. Slowest after María: Vieques (26 months), Maunabo (25 months), Salinas (20 months); fastest: Hormigueros (2 months), San Germán (2 months), Cabo Rojo (3 months). After Fiona 77 of 78 municipios were back by October. Barrios after María: half took 8 months or less, one in ten 18 or more.
caveats: Light is a proxy for power and activity, not a count of homes with power: it includes streetlights, businesses and traffic. Say 'light came back', not 'power came back'.
A long time can mean a lasting change rather than a long outage: homes left empty, a business that closed, or streetlights changed to LED (whiter light, which the sensor sees less of).
Each month is a composite of its clear nights, so an outage of a few days or weeks barely shows. Fiona's island-wide blackout lasted days to weeks for most customers, so most areas read 1 month.
The 80% line and the two months are the observatory's rule. With 70% the island reads 6 months after María, with 90% 14; the barrio median moves from 6 to 13 months.

Check: by the rule the island's light was back by 2018-05 after María; the Army Corps of Engineers reported 98.4% of the utility's customers restored in mid-May 2018. After Fiona it was back by 2022-10; LUMA reported 90% of customers restored on 2022-10-01. EAGLE-I's outage record (Oak Ridge National Laboratory, CC BY 4.0, figshare 24237376, 2022 file) agrees by region: in each of the seven LUMA regions the customers out fell to 10% of the peak or fewer between 2022-09-29 (San Juan, Bayamón, Carolina) and 2022-10-10 (Mayagüez), the southwest last, so every region was mostly back within October.

The rule is the observatory's; the island's figures agree with the utility's record of customers restored (docs/storm_recovery.md).
storm_recovery.storm_low_light_pct.method: storm_recovery.py reads the observatory's monthly night-time light (nightlights_monthly.json: NASA Black Marble VNP46A3, pixels of about 460 m pooled by barrio, municipio and Puerto Rico) and compares each month after the storm month (September) with the same calendar month in the twelve months before it, so that cloudy and clear seasons cancel out. Light counts as back in the first month when it and the next month are both at least 80% of the same month the year before; the figure counts months from September. The lowest month is the darkest from September to March, as a share of the same month the year before. An area whose mean in the year before is under 0.5 nW/cm²/sr has no figure: its light moves 20% to 70% from month to month without any storm. No network and no key: the file is rebuilt with the night-light file.
storm_recovery.storm_low_light_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 27% of the year before after María, 81% after Fiona. Darkest after María: Adjuntas (2%), Orocovis (3%), Ciales (4%). Darkest after Fiona: Maricao (41%), Adjuntas (57%), Guánica (58%), in the southwest where Fiona came ashore.
caveats: Light is a proxy for power and activity, not a count of homes with power: it includes streetlights, businesses and traffic. Say 'light came back', not 'power came back'.

Each month is a composite of its clear nights, so an outage of a few days or weeks barely shows. Fiona's island-wide blackout lasted days to weeks for most customers, so most areas read 1 month. The storm month mixes nights before and after the storm, which is why Fiona's lowest month reads well above zero.
Pixels are about 460 m across and light spills over borders, so a small barrio next to a bright one reads brighter than it was.
storm_recovery.storm_low_light_pct.source_detail: Calculated by the observatory from NASA Black Marble VNP46A3 (collection 2) monthly night-time light, as read by nightlights.py (pixels of about 460 m, pooled by barrio, municipio and Puerto Rico); Román et al. (2018)

boundaries.wcrp_estado.plain: Whether the community's resilience plan is approved by the Puerto Rico Department of Housing or still in progress.
boundaries.wcrp_estado.plain_es: Si el Departamento de la Vivienda (PRDOH) aprobó el plan de resiliencia de la comunidad o si todavía está en proceso.
boundaries.wcrp_estado.definition: The estado field: plan_aprobado for 59 communities and en_proceso for 17 (10 in the WCRP program list and 7 phase-1 communities from the program's tracker), as of 2026-10-06.
boundaries.wcrp_estado.how_to_read: On the map, each community is marked with the center figure of the WCRP program logo: solid orange for an approved plan and an orange outline for a plan in progress. When several plans share a point, the marker is solid if any of them is approved; the popup lists each one with its own marker.
caveats: A snapshot of 2026-10-06. Plans approved later show as in progress until FPR updates the CSV.

boundaries.wcrp_ubicacion.plain: What the dot for a WCRP community is placed on, and the name of that place, so you can judge how close it is to the community.
boundaries.wcrp_ubicacion.plain_es: Sobre qué está colocado el punto de una comunidad de WCRP, y el nombre de ese lugar, para poder juzgar qué tan cerca está de la comunidad.
boundaries.wcrp_ubicacion.definition: The ubicacion field gives the kind of place and referencia gives its name. In the 2026-10-06 list: 40 osm, 23 comunidad_especial, 7 pueblo, 4 barrio_censo and 2 manual.
boundaries.wcrp_ubicacion.method: wcrp.py fills both fields when it matches a name. When FPR places a row by hand, ubicacion still names the kind of place the point comes from, and the CSV's nota column (not published) says why and cites the plan.
boundaries.wcrp_ubicacion.how_to_read: A comunidad_especial point is usually inside the community. An osm or barrio_censo point can be a kilometer or more away when the community is one sector of a large barrio.
caveats: None of these places is the community's own boundary. Some landmarks, such as a school the plan names, may sit just outside it.

values.comunidad_especial: A point inside the Comunidad Especial with that name (Junta de Planificación, 2006).

values.barrio_censo: A point inside the Census barrio with that name.
values.pueblo: The town center of the municipality.
values.manual: Coordinates that the plan itself gives.
